etymology: Hebrew Yarmuth, “height” or “elevation,” an Amorite royal city in the lowland of Judah.
biblical_def: Jarmuth was one of the royal cities of the Amorites, whose king Piram joined the confederacy of five kings that warred against Gibeon for making peace with Israel. When the Gibeonites by their craft had obtained a league with Joshua, Adonizedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron, and to Piram king of Jarmuth, and to Japhia king of Lachish, and to Debir king of Eglon, saying, “Come up unto me, and help me, that we may smite Gibeon” (Jos 10:3–5). The LORD discomfited them before Israel and slew them with a great slaughter at Gibeon, casting down great stones from heaven upon them as they fled. The five kings hid in the cave at Makkedah, and were brought out and slain and hanged on five trees, Piram of Jarmuth among them (Jos 10:23–26). The king of Jarmuth is named again in the roll of the one and thirty kings whom Joshua smote on the west of Jordan (Jos 12:11). The city itself fell within the inheritance of the tribe of Judah, numbered in the lowland towns of their allotment (Jos 15:35). Jarmuth stands as a witness that the LORD God of Israel fought for His people, casting down the proud kings of Canaan, and giving the land He had sworn to the fathers into the hand of His covenant nation, city by city and king by king.
webster_summary: An Amorite royal city of the Judahite lowland; its king Piram joined the war against Gibeon and was slain by Joshua.

etymology: Hebrew Yuttah, “inclined” or “extended,” a town in the hill country of Judah given to the priests.
biblical_def: Juttah was a town in the mountainous south of the inheritance of Judah, numbered among the cities of the hill country in the roll of Judah’s allotment: “And Maon, Carmel, and Ziph, and Juttah” (Jos 15:55). When the Levites received their portion among the tribes, having no inheritance of land but the LORD Himself, Juttah was one of the cities given out of the tribe of Judah to the children of Aaron the priest, that they might dwell scattered through Israel and teach the people the law of God (Jos 21:16). Thus a town of the Judahite hills became a dwelling place of the priesthood, a small seat of the worship and instruction of the LORD set in the midst of the tribe of the kings. Some have thought it the city of Judah in the hill country to which Mary went to visit Elisabeth, the home of Zacharias the priest, though the Scripture there names only “a city of Juda” (Luke 1:39). Juttah stands as a quiet witness that the LORD, who gave the land to His people, also planted the priests among the tribes, that no part of the inheritance should be without the presence of those appointed to keep and teach His word. The faithfulness of God in the allotment reached even to the obscure towns of the hills.

etymology: Hebrew Eshtemoa, “place of hearing” or “obedience,” a Levitical city in the hill country of Judah.
biblical_def: Eshtemoa was a town in the hill country of the inheritance of Judah, given to the Levites for their dwelling. When the children of Aaron received their cities out of the tribes of Judah and Simeon, Eshtemoa with her suburbs was numbered among them, a priestly city set apart for the servants of the sanctuary (Jos 21:14; 1Ch 6:57). Though the Levites had no portion of land like their brethren, the LORD being their inheritance, they were given towns such as Eshtemoa scattered through Israel, that the worship and teaching of God might dwell in the midst of every tribe. Eshtemoa comes into view again in the days of David’s wandering, when he smote the Amalekites who had burned Ziklag and carried away the wives and goods of his men. Recovering all the spoil, David sent of it as a present to the elders of Judah, to his friends, “to them which were in Eshtemoa” among the others (1Sa 30:28). Thus the town shared in the bounty of the man after God’s own heart, who in his rising remembered the towns that had befriended him in his affliction. Eshtemoa, whose name means “place of hearing,” stands as a fitting seat for the Levites whose office was to make the people hear and obey the law of the LORD; and as a witness to the kindness of David, who shared the spoil with the cities of his God.

etymology: Hebrew Yattir, “pre-eminent” or “abundant,” a Levitical town in the hill country of Judah.
biblical_def: Jattir was a town in the mountainous part of the inheritance of Judah, named in the roll of the hill-country cities of their allotment: “And in the mountains, Shamir, and Jattir, and Socoh” (Jos 15:48). Like Eshtemoa near which it lay, Jattir was given to the Levites for their dwelling, numbered among the cities of the children of Aaron the priest out of the tribe of Judah, that the servants of the sanctuary might dwell scattered through the land (Jos 21:14; 1Ch 6:57). It comes into view again in the latter days of David’s wandering, when he had smitten the Amalekites and recovered all that they had carried from Ziklag. Out of the spoil he sent presents to the elders of Judah, to the towns that had befriended him in his outlaw years, and Jattir was among them: “and to them which were in Jattir” (1Sa 30:27). Thus this obscure hill town of the priests shared in the kindness of the Lord’s anointed in the day of his rising. Jattir stands as another witness to the faithfulness of God in the allotment of the land, who gave to every tribe its portion and to the Levites their cities; and to the gracious memory of David, who in his exaltation remembered with gifts the towns that had sheltered and loved him in his affliction.

etymology: Hebrew Maqqedah, perhaps “place of shepherds” or “herding place,” a town of the Judahite lowland.
biblical_def: Makkedah was a town in the lowland of Judah, made memorable by the cave wherein the five Amorite kings hid themselves in the day of the LORD’s great victory at Gibeon. When the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon fled before Israel, they hid in the cave at Makkedah; and it was told Joshua, who commanded great stones to be rolled upon the mouth of the cave and men set to keep it, while Israel pursued and smote their enemies (Jos 10:16–21). Then Joshua bade them open the cave and bring out the five kings, and he laid his foot upon their necks before the captains of his men of war, saying, “Fear not, nor be dismayed, be strong and of good courage: for thus shall the LORD do to all your enemies” (Jos 10:25). He smote them and slew them, and hanged them on five trees until the evening, and at sundown cast their bodies into the cave and laid great stones upon its mouth. That same day Joshua took Makkedah, and smote it with the edge of the sword, doing to its king as he had done to the king of Jericho (Jos 10:28). The town is numbered afterward among the cities of Judah in the lowland (Jos 15:41). Makkedah stands as one of the great monuments of the conquest, where the LORD made plain that He fights for His people and treads down their proud enemies; and the foot of Joshua upon the necks of the kings is a figure of the victory of the greater Joshua over every power of darkness.
webster_summary: A town of the Judahite lowland whose cave hid the five Amorite kings, whom Joshua slew and hanged.

etymology: Hebrew Mareshah, “summit” or “place at the head,” a town in the lowland of Judah.
biblical_def: Mareshah was a town in the lowland, or Shephelah, of the inheritance of Judah, named in the roll of the valley cities of their allotment (Jos 15:44). It became famous as the place of one of the great deliverances of the LORD wrought for His people. When Zerah the Ethiopian came out against Judah with a host of a thousand thousand and three hundred chariots, King Asa set his battle in array in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah. And Asa cried unto the LORD his God, and said, “LORD, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O LORD our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude” (2Ch 14:11). So the LORD smote the Ethiopians before Asa and before Judah, and they fled, and were destroyed before the LORD and before His host; and Judah carried away very much spoil. Mareshah was afterward fortified by Rehoboam (2Ch 11:8), and the prophet Micah, lamenting the judgment coming upon the land, named it in a play upon its meaning: “Yet will I bring an heir unto thee, O inhabitant of Mareshah” (Mic 1:15). Mareshah stands as a witness that the battle is the LORD’s, and that He saves not by the multitude of an host but by His own arm; when His people rest wholly upon Him and go forth in His name, He gives them the victory over the strongest of their foes.
webster_summary: A town of the Judahite lowland where Asa cried to the LORD and the host of Zerah the Ethiopian was smitten.

etymology: Hebrew Netsib, “pillar” or “garrison,” a town in the lowland of Judah.
biblical_def: Nezib was a town in the valley, or lowland, of the inheritance of Judah, named in the roll of the Shephelah cities of their allotment: “And Keilah, and Achzib, and Mareshah; nine cities with their villages” — and among the nearby towns, “And Nezib” (Jos 15:43). It is a place of which the Scripture records little more than its name and its place in the lists of Judah’s towns, one of the many cities given into the hand of the tribe of the kings when the LORD divided the land. Yet its very inclusion in the inspired record is not in vain, for the careful naming of even the obscure towns of the lowland testifies to the exactness of God’s gift. The name Nezib, “pillar” or “garrison,” speaks of a fixed and settled place, a fortified post in the borderland between the hill country and the plain. Nezib stands as a quiet witness that the LORD performed His promise to the fathers down to the least of its particulars, planting Judah in town after town of the land of Canaan. No city was too small to be numbered in the allotment, and no word of God’s covenant promise fell to the ground; the obscure towns no less than the great ones declare the faithfulness of Him who gave His people their inheritance.

etymology: Hebrew Beth-tappuach, “house of the apple” or “place of apples,” a town in the hill country of Judah.
biblical_def: Beth-tappuah was a town in the mountainous part of the inheritance of Judah, named in the roll of the hill-country cities of their allotment: “And Humtah, and Kirjatharba, which is Hebron, and Zior” — and among the towns of that quarter, “Tappuah, and Aphekah, and Humtah” and Beth-tappuah (Jos 15:53). Its name, “house of the apple” or “place of apples,” speaks of a fruitful and pleasant spot in the highlands near Hebron, where the orchards bore their fruit upon the slopes of the hills of Judah. The Scripture records little beyond its name and its place among the cities of the inheritance, one of the many towns given into the hand of Judah when the LORD divided the land of Canaan among the tribes. Yet the very naming of Beth-tappuah in the inspired record bears its witness, for the careful lists of Joshua leave none of the towns of the allotment unnumbered. Beth-tappuah stands as a quiet token of the goodness of the land the LORD gave His people, a land of hills and valleys, of orchards and springs, flowing with milk and honey as He had promised the fathers. The very name of the “house of apples” recalls that the inheritance God gave was no barren waste but a good and fruitful land, the gift of His covenant faithfulness to the seed of Abraham.

corruption_summary: A place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to God’s faithfulness in giving His people a good and fruitful land.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God’s faithfulness in giving the land tribe by tribe, even to its obscure and fruitful hill towns. Beth-tappuah, the “house of apples,” was one of the highland cities near Hebron numbered in Judah’s allotment. Its very name recalls the goodness of the inheritance the LORD gave, a land of orchards and springs flowing with milk and honey, no barren waste but the good gift promised to the fathers and bestowed in covenant faithfulness upon their seed.

Beth-tappuah also stands against the skepticism that would dissolve the conquest into legend, for the careful naming of even so small a town as the “house of apples” marks the record as true history set in real country. And the fruitful land of Judah pictures the inheritance of the saints in Christ, who go up to possess a better country, that is, an heavenly, prepared for them by their God. As Judah received a good land of hills and orchards, so the believer’s portion in the greater Joshua is a fruitful and abiding inheritance that cannot fade away.

etymology: Hebrew Anab, “grape” or “place of grapes,” a town in the hill country of Judah.
biblical_def: Anab was a town in the mountainous part of the inheritance of Judah, named in the roll of the hill-country cities of their allotment: “And Arab, and Dumah, and Eshean, and Janum, and Bethtappuah” — and among the towns, “And Anab” (Jos 15:50). It is remembered chiefly as one of the cities from which Joshua cut off the Anakim, the giant race whose great stature had so terrified the spies in the days of Moses. For when Joshua had taken the whole land, “at that time came Joshua, and cut off the Anakims from the mountains, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the mountains of Judah, and from all the mountains of Israel: Joshua destroyed them utterly with their cities” (Jos 11:21). Thus the very giants whom Israel had feared, saying they were as grasshoppers in their sight, were driven out and destroyed by the LORD through His servant Joshua; and Anab, once a stronghold of the Anakim, was given into the inheritance of Judah. The name Anab, “grape,” recalls the fruitful highlands near Hebron whence the spies had brought the great cluster of grapes from the brook of Eshcol. Anab stands as a witness that the LORD is mightier than the giants that affright His people; the strongholds that seemed impregnable He casts down, and gives His people the inheritance He has promised, though the sons of Anak stood in the way.

corruption_summary: A place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the LORD’s faithfulness in casting down the giants that affright His people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God’s faithfulness in giving the land, casting down even the giants the spies had feared. Anab was a stronghold of the Anakim, the great race whose stature had once made Israel say they were as grasshoppers; yet Joshua cut off the Anakim from Anab and all the mountains of Judah, and the city fell into the inheritance. What seemed impossible to unbelief the LORD performed; the giants that affrighted the ten spies were no match for the God who fought for His people.

The casting down of the Anakim from Anab typifies the believer’s inheritance and warfare in Christ, the greater Joshua. The strongholds and giants that stand between the saint and his promised rest are not too great for the Lord, who goes before His people to dispossess them. As Caleb, who wholly followed the LORD, drove the sons of Anak from Hebron, so the believer who trusts his God overcomes the powers that would bar him from the inheritance, for greater is He that is in us than the giants of the land.

etymology: Hebrew Gedor, “a wall” or “fortified place,” a town in the hill country of Judah.
biblical_def: Gedor was a town in the mountainous part of the inheritance of Judah, named in the roll of the hill-country cities of their allotment: “Maarath, and Bethanoth, and Eltekon; six cities with their villages: Halhul, Bethzur, and Gedor” (Jos 15:58). Its name, “a wall” or “fortified place,” speaks of a walled town set upon the heights of Judah, between Hebron and Bethlehem. The Chronicler records that the families of Simeon, seeking pasture for their flocks, went to the entrance of Gedor, “unto the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks. And they found fat pasture and good, and the land was wide, and quiet, and peaceable” (1Ch 4:39–40); there they smote the inhabitants and dwelt in their rooms, finding rest for their flocks in the good land. Thus Gedor and its valley appear as a place of fat pasture and quietness in the hill country, a token of the goodness of the inheritance the LORD gave His people. The Scripture records little else of the town beyond its name and its place among the cities of Judah, yet its very inclusion in the inspired lists bears witness to the exactness of God’s gift. Gedor stands as a quiet monument that the LORD divided the land down to its least towns, planting His people in a country of walled cities and fat pastures, and performing to the seed of Abraham all that He had sworn to the fathers.

corruption_summary: A place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to God’s faithfulness in giving His people a land of walled cities and fat pastures.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God’s faithfulness in giving the land tribe by tribe, down to its walled hill towns and quiet valleys. Gedor was a fortified town of the Judahite highlands, and at the entrance of its valley the Simeonites found fat pasture and good, a land wide and quiet and peaceable. The LORD who divided the inheritance gave His people a good country of cities and pastures, performing to the seed of Abraham all that He had sworn to the fathers.

The naming of Gedor also stands against the skepticism that would dissolve the conquest into legend, for the careful record of its place in Judah’s allotment and the Simeonites’ resting at its valley is the precision of true history, not of myth. And the fat and quiet pasture the Simeonites found pictures the rest the LORD gives His people in the inheritance He prepares. As the flocks of Simeon found a land wide and peaceable at Gedor, so the saints find rest for their souls in the good land of promise secured for them by the greater Joshua, the Lord Jesus Christ.
